title: The grain of wheat (John 12:24)
hook: unless the grain falls and dies, it stays alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, nard poured out, and a house full of its scent. Your line was the whole house knew.

A packet of seeds can sit in a kitchen drawer for years. Open it, and the seeds are all still there, a bit drier. Nothing has gone wrong, exactly. Nothing has happened at all. Put one in the dirt, and it stops being a seed. It splits, it disappears into roots and a stalk, and if you're lucky, a whole head of grain. Jesus is in Jerusalem now, with the Passover close, and some Greeks have come asking to see him. His answer is about a seed.
screen: `SEEDS IN A DRAWER.` → `ONE IN THE DIRT.` → `SOME GREEKS ASK TO SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Some Greeks, Gentiles in the Douay, people who had come up to worship at the feast, find Philip: Sir, we would see Jesus. Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus. Then Jesus says the hour has come. All through John, his hour has been not yet; at Cana, my hour is not yet come. Now, when outsiders arrive wanting to see him, the hour is here. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Notice the word alone. The opposite of bearing fruit, here, isn't failure. It's staying alone, intact and unchanged. A grain that keeps itself is safe, and it's by itself forever. Jesus is talking first about his own death. Readers hear an answer to the Greeks in it: a few lines on he says, if I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself. Then he widens it: he that loveth his life shall lose it, and he that hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal. Some readers hear hate there as a strong Semitic way of saying, don't cling. Early Christians took the seed picture straight to the martyrs. Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed: the more they're cut down, the more they grow. Catholics also hear it in smaller deaths: a pride let go, a grudge buried, an evening given up.
screen: `WE WOULD SEE JESUS.` · `THE HOUR HAS COME.` · `UNLESS IT DIE, IT STAYS ALONE.` · `THE BLOOD OF CHRISTIANS IS SEED.` · then, large: `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT.`

segments.voice: Open your hands on your lap and breathe, and find one small self-interest from today: needing to win an argument, the last word, the bigger slice, the credit. Picture it leaving your hands and going into the ground. If you pray, hold the line, if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit; if not, keep your hands open and breathe.
The grain of wheat. Jesus's picture of his own death: a seed that stays alone unless it falls, and bears much fruit when it does. Today's word.
Your line: falls and bears fruit. The grain falls, and the field comes later. Day five hundred fifteen, done.

howItsDone: The Church reads John 12:20–33 on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year B, and on the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr.

chat.says: Why did Jesus answer the Greeks who wanted to see him by talking about a seed?
options: His hour had come: like a grain that dies and bears fruit, his death would draw all to him.
He was putting them off: his hour had not yet come, so outsiders would have to wait.
He meant his teaching would spread slowly, with no need for anyone to die.
chat.meaning: The hour had come. Unless the grain dies it remains alone; if it dies, much fruit. Lifted up, he will draw all things to himself.

Gentiles.meaning: people who aren't Jewish; the Douay's word for these Greeks

Cana.meaning: the wedding town where Jesus said, my hour is not yet come

Semitic.meaning: here, the Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking in strong contrasts

Tertullian.meaning: an early Christian writer: the blood of Christians is seed

notes: 'Sir, we would see Jesus' and 'he that loveth his life…' are given without quotation marks, close to Douay wording.
Tertullian, Apology 50 (c. 197): 'the blood of Christians is seed', paraphrased. Confirm date and reference.
'Hate' as a Semitic idiom for preferring less / not clinging: common reading. Confirm.
John 12:20–33 on Fifth Sunday of Lent (Year B) and John 12:24–26 on the feast of St. Lawrence. Confirm.
